pr.title: Don't check unsize goal in MIR validation when opaques remain
pr.description: Similarly to `mir_assign_valid_types`, let's just skip when there are opaques. Fixes #130921.
pr.author: compiler-errors

processing.reason: PR #130989 changes only the MIR `Validator`'s handling of unsize predicates that mention opaque types. Before the fix, `predicate_must_hold_modulo_regions` tried to prove such a predicate and falsely reported broken MIR/ICE; after the fix it skips those predicates and accepts the valid MIR. Neither revision changes the runtime semantics of any Rust program: the new regression test is a compile-only `//@ check-pass` test with `-Zvalidate-mir`, and the dead-branch unsize coercion never executes. There is no source-level value transformation here, so no pair of ordinary Rust functions with identical inputs can faithfully show different defined runtime results under Miri. Modeling the validator's boolean accept/reject decision would be a synthetic abstraction of compiler internals, not the historical program rewrite the test harness is meant to validate, and would risk manufacturing an unrelated difference. Both pre-fix and post-fix compiled programs have the same observable behavior when validation does not ICE.

evidence: Don't check unsize goal in MIR validation when opaques remain
We sometimes have to use `defining_opaque_types` for predicates
It is harmless enough to just not validate anything
Unsize coercion, but `&Foo<[impl Sized; 2]>` isn't coercible to `&Foo<[i32]>`
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historically incorrect validation behavior was to check unsize goals containing opaque types exactly like ordinary predicates, without using `defining_opaque_types`. For valid MIR involving an RPIT array of `impl Sized`, this produced a false broken-MIR result such as `Unsize coercion, but &Foo<[impl Sized; 2]> isn't coercible to &Foo<[i32]>`, causing an ICE. The corrected behavior is to skip the obligation check when the predicate has opaque types and accept it, rather than treating the opaque-containing predicate as a failed coercion.
analysis.inputDomain: Rust programs compiled with `-Zvalidate-mir`, especially functions returning opaque types via RPIT, where MIR contains an unsize coercion from an array/opaque type to a concrete unsized type, including coercions in unreachable/dead branches. The regression shape is an RPIT return such as `[impl Sized; N]` or a reference to it, coerced to a slice/reference with a concrete element type.
analysis.originalLogic: The Validator checked an unsize coercion by registering the corresponding unsize predicate as an obligation in a fresh inference context and reporting broken MIR when that obligation did not hold. This validation is intended to confirm that MIR unsize casts are legal after a pass.
pitfalls: Do not skip all unsize validation; skip only predicates for which `has_opaque_types()` is true, so ordinary invalid unsize casts remain detectable.
Upcast the generic predicate to `ty::Predicate` before calling `has_opaque_types()`.
Opaque types are revealed after analysis; the source comment says it is harmless not to validate opaque-containing predicates because validation still happens later, when opaques have been revealed.
A failed validator obligation is a validation false positive/ICE here, not evidence that the MIR coercion should be rejected by type checking.
Do not conflate this with borrow-check or post-copy overwrite issues; the trigger is specifically an unsize goal mentioning opaque types.
preconditions: The program uses an opaque type (RPIT/`impl Trait`) inside the source type of an unsize coercion.
MIR validation is enabled, e.g. with `-Zvalidate-mir`.
The validator evaluates the unsize predicate without supplying `defining_opaque_types`, so proving the opaque-containing predicate fails.
The coercion may be in a branch that is never executed; validation still examines the MIR.
analysis.summary: MIR validation must not prove unsize goals that still mention opaque types. The old Validator treated such goals as ordinary obligations and falsely rejected valid RPIT unsize coercions, producing a broken-MIR ICE. The fix upcasts the predicate, skips validation when `pred.has_opaque_types()`, and keeps the check for predicates without opaques.
analysis.testStrategy: Add a UI `check-pass` regression test compiled with `-Zvalidate-mir` that reproduces an RPIT unsize coercion, e.g. a function returning `&'static [impl Sized; 0]` and containing `let _: &[i32] = x;` in a dead branch. Keep a concrete/non-opaque control case with the same unsize coercion shape to show ordinary unsize casts still validate, and consider a negative control with an invalid non-opaque unsize cast to confirm the skip is not blanket. The historical crash test was removed and replaced by this check-pass UI test; no compiler execution is needed beyond the compile-check.
analysis.trigger: Running MIR validation on a MIR unsize coercion whose predicate mentions an opaque type, for example `Foo<[impl Sized; 2]>` being coerced to `&Foo<[i32]>` while the opaque type is not yet resolved in the validation inference context.
